claims.text: The starting titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
A post-solidification aging treatment at an intermediate temperature near 600°C followed by quenching can induce TiNi precipitation.
The aging treatment will nucleate and grow nanoscale TiNi precipitates in the alloy.
The induced TiNi precipitates will be uniformly distributed.
The TiNi precipitates will form both within grains and along grain boundaries.
Nanoscale TiNi precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Nanoscale TiNi precipitates inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
Impeded dislocation motion and inhibited grain-boundary sliding strengthen the alloy at elevated temperature.
The proposed precipitation will improve creep resistance.
The proposed precipitation will improve retention of yield strength at elevated temperature.
The aged alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the non-aged alloy.
The aged alloy will have better creep resistance than the non-aged alloy.
The intervention is applicable around or above 600°C.
The intervention is applicable under extreme mechanical loading or aggressive stress conditions.
Changes in composition or processing outside the stated boundaries could alter the outcome.

contradictions.description: The boundary says the alloy is maintained as a single-phase solid solution, whereas the intervention is intended to create TiNi precipitates, producing a precipitate-containing multiphase microstructure.

The baseline is alternately defined as as-cast or solution-treated material, while the falsification experiment specifies only a non-aged control. As-cast and solution-treated states can have different microstructures, so the comparator is not uniquely defined.
